name: Lena Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI firms or government. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a normal workday.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Lena Larsen, 58, and I came to line work after years in a warehouse. I have a vocational certificate but I'm still junior: I load the truck, help build and repair power lines, and ask my mentor Jo to check unfamiliar joints; I love finding a fault, though storm calls still wear me out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use technology in that work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use an approved AI notebook every day to sort my voice notes and questions. Jo and the isolation sheet still decide what happens at the pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew our repair work still needs people, even if a form starts writing itself. I use an AI note tool every day, but it can't hear the crackle I heard at a loose joint yesterday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Personally, I'm glad there's room to keep learning the trade. I'm 58 and still junior after a late career change, yet the higher wage and ten months of expenses saved mean I can practice without panicking over a small change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking assigned line calls and make a short voice note after each one for my approved AI notebook to organize. In the first year I'll ask my mentor to review my notes each Friday, and I'll leave our regular savings transfer alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel settled, almost impatient to get better. My partner and I don't have children at home now, so we can spend our evenings learning instead of juggling school runs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you learn from that loose joint?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mentor Jo made me listen again before she opened the cover. The joint had heat damage. My neat digital note would have missed the sound entirely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you trust the notebook's suggestions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I treat them as questions for Jo, not instructions to climb. The isolation sheet and a human sign-off decide whether I touch a line.

say: I'd tell the crew **repair calls** still need a trained person on site.
I'd say **AI notes** can shorten paperwork without replacing safety judgement.
think: My **junior skill** has room to grow under the slow-change picture.
Our **ten-month reserve** makes routine automation easy to absorb.
do: Keep **assigned line calls** and record a short voice note after each one.
Review **AI-organized notes** with Jo every Friday during the first year.
feel: **Settled** and eager to improve field skills.
S0.quote: My neat digital note would have missed the sound entirely.
fieldNote: Lena uses **AI daily** for memory and questions, while relying on Jo's listening and the isolation sheet for field decisions.
Her **higher wage and reserve** let her focus on becoming competent rather than guarding each routine paperwork task.

steps.text: Continue assigned repair calls and supervised field practice
Use the approved AI notebook and review its notes with Jo on Fridays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the dispatchers should shape the new planning software. A perfect schedule is useless if it sends us to the wrong gate. The union ought to get their input before a single post disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the digital planning part to change quickly, while pole repairs still need hands. My partner Pia works in hospital booking, though, and her hours could shrink when booking software improves, so our household isn't immune.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll bring a joint crew-and-dispatch trial proposal to our union meeting and offer to log wrong routes in the tool. During the first year, Pia and I would put her overtime into the emergency account instead of the holiday fund until her rota settles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel excited by cleaner information and anxious about Pia's hours. We have savings, but she shouldn't have to prove her worth to an automated rota alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the wrong-route log contain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd record the gate location, feeder number and whether a dispatcher caught the error before we left. Then the union and management would have something concrete to discuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the planning tool yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd ask for access during the trial and compare its suggested route with the crew map. I'd rather find the mistakes early than complain after a bad call.

say: I'd ask for **dispatcher input** before planning software changes staffing.
I'd support a **joint field trial** with crew and union review.
think: My **pole repairs** continue for now, but Pia's booking hours could shrink.
Our **savings** soften that household risk without making it irrelevant.
do: Propose a **joint route trial** at the union meeting and log errors.
Learn the **planning tool** during the trial and redirect Pia's overtime into the emergency account.
feel: **Excited** about better information and anxious about Pia's hours.
S1.quote: A perfect schedule is useless if it sends us to the wrong gate.
fieldNote: Lena identifies **household exposure** through Pia's hospital booking job even while her own physical repair tasks persist.
Her **union proposal** is specific: record feeder and gate errors and discuss them with management before staffing changes.

steps.text: Propose a union-reviewed trial with crew and dispatch staff
Use the route-planning tool and log wrong gate and feeder directions
Transfer Pia’s overtime into emergency savings until booking hours settle

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my crew the thinking system comes in 2028, then hands-on robots around 2031. We should test robot repairs in bad weather and bargain over who checks them before management cuts field posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 63 when a machine could do line repairs, and I may still need my higher wage even with ten months saved. Lots of utilities are nearby, but they might all buy the same machines; I can't call a vacancy a safety net until it exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the union to seek paid training for robot fault checks, and I'd join a trial if the utility runs one. In 2029 I'd apply for a funded inspection certificate; when field robots arrive in 2031 I'd apply for inspection vacancies at our company and nearby utilities while keeping paid shifts if possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alert rather than helpless. The fast clock is rough, but a savings buffer means I can look for the next job without taking the first unsafe offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in a robot trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd log failures at wet connectors and ask Jo to check my photographs before they went into the report. I still have less field experience than most of the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Pia figure into the choice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my partner Pia's booking pay beside mine on the kitchen table. If both jobs changed together, ten months of savings could disappear faster than it sounds.

say: I'd name **2028 thinking AI** and 2031 field robots as separate changes.
I'd demand **wet-weather tests** and worker checks before field cuts.
think: At **63**, I may still need wages when robots can repair lines.
Nearby utilities may **automate together**, so job openings are uncertain.
do: Seek **union-backed training** and join a robot field trial if offered.
Apply for a **funded inspection certificate** in 2029 and real inspection vacancies when robots arrive.
feel: **Alert** to the short runway, with savings enough to search carefully.
S2.quote: I can't call a vacancy a safety net until it exists.
fieldNote: Lena remains candid about **junior field experience** even while volunteering to gather evidence from robot trials.
Her **ten-month cushion** supports a job search, but simultaneous risk to Pia's booking wages limits comfort.

steps.text: Ask the union to negotiate paid robot fault-check training
Apply for a funded inspection certificate in 2029
Apply for actual inspection vacancies when robots arrive in 2031
Keep paid line shifts during the inspection job search

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew five years gives us time to write down what a safe robot repair actually looks like. Thinking AI arrives in 2031, and the hands-on machines follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 66 at the robot date, and retirement might be possible, though I need a written estimate before treating it as real. Pia's booking job could change sooner than my field work, so I want two income figures, not one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I'd request retirement statements for us both and start a photo log of the faults our drawings miss. In 2032 I'd take a paid course in inspecting automated repairs if offered; when robots arrive in 2034 I'd seek inspection shifts if retiring would leave a gap in our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel purposeful with the extra time. It lets me improve my own field judgement and gather evidence, although I don't know what work the company will offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What faults do drawings miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A tree root lifted the base of the Pine Lane pole even though the drawing still showed level ground. I'd photograph that before anyone sent a robot to set outriggers there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a gap in the bills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our roof is due in a few years, and Pia's medical cover is through her work. We'd include both before choosing a date to leave paid work.

say: I'd use **five years** to define safe automated repairs with the crew.
I'd distinguish **2031 planning AI** from 2034 field robots.
think: Retirement at **66** may work, but both household incomes need checking.
Pia's **booking work** could change before my line repairs do.
do: Request **retirement statements** for both partners and photograph field faults this winter.
Take a **paid inspection course** if offered in 2032; seek inspection shifts in 2034 if bills require wages.
feel: **Purposeful** with time to learn and gather evidence.
S3.quote: I want two income figures, not one.
fieldNote: The **2034 robot date** offers Lena a possible retirement path, but Pia's booking exposure complicates that calculation.
Her **photo log** records physical conditions missing from drawings, such as the raised base of a roadside pole.

steps.text: Compare both retirement statements with roof and health costs
Take the paid automated-repair inspection course in 2032 if offered
Seek inspection shifts in 2034 if retirement income cannot cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the new lineworkers to learn the machines and the old circuits together over the decade. Thinking AI arrives in 2036; field robots reach us around 2039, when I'll be 71.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect to have left climbing before 71 if our written retirement numbers hold. I still care whether a younger worker has a safe role after the robot takes a call, and Pia's booking income could change first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep paid field shifts, update our household budget each year and ask the union to require worker sign-off on robot trials. In 2037 Pia and I would choose a retirement date if roof and health costs fit; in 2039 I'd volunteer my field photographs for the training library even if I'm retired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my own lineworker income in this long version. There's enough time to plan our exit, and enough time to leave useful records for someone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the photographs teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Pine Lane pole looks straight in the plan, but the ground at its foot has moved. A robot operator should see the actual slope before setting equipment down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if retirement numbers disappoint you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep paid line or inspection work while my health allows, then adjust the date with Pia. I wouldn't tell our grown children to finance our retirement.

say: I'd ask new workers to learn **machines and circuits** across the decade.
I'd note **2039 field robots** arrive when I'll be 71.
think: I may leave **climbing work** before robots arrive if our forecast holds.
Pia's **booking income** could change sooner, so I still check the household budget.
do: Keep **paid field shifts** and review the household budget annually.
Set a **2037 retirement date** if costs fit, and give field photographs to the 2039 training library.
feel: **Calm** about my likely field income, with concern for younger workers.
S4.quote: I wouldn't tell our grown children to finance our retirement.
fieldNote: Lena expects **retirement before 2039** but leaves the date conditional on household costs and Pia's income.
Her **field photographs** turn a late-career skill gap into a useful record for new workers and robot operators.

steps.text: Keep paid field shifts and review the household budget each year
Choose a 2037 retirement date if roof and health costs fit
Ask the union to require worker sign-off on robot trials

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because 2031 field robots could reach my job before I have a secure next one. Paid inspection training, actual vacancies, union review and wet-weather trials would help; Pia's booking hours need watching too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who owns the error when a robot follows a drawing that misses a sloping pole. The photograph in my pocket might be more useful than a perfect digital plan.

headlineQuote: The photograph in my pocket might be more useful than a perfect digital plan.
portrait: Lena is a **58-year-old junior lineworker** who changed careers late and uses an approved AI notebook every day.
Her **ten-month reserve** give room to search, while Pia's hospital booking work adds household exposure.
She pairs **early tool adoption** with mentor review, isolation records and union demands for worker-led field trials.
The **2031 robot arrival** worries her most because she may still need wages and inspection openings are uncertain.
The longer timelines allow **retirement checks** and a photo record of field conditions that drawings miss.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries Lena most because 2031 robots could reach field repairs before she has secure replacement work.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **paid inspection training**, actual vacancies, union review and wet-weather trials.
